Every lens makes two important planes: the back focal plane, where all rays leaving the sample in the same direction meet (this is the diffraction pattern), and the image plane, where rays from the same point of the sample meet (this is the image). The TEM switches between modes by changing which one the next lens shows on the screen.

Imaging and diffraction modes in TEM
Imaging modeDiffraction mode
Intermediate lens focused onImage plane of the objective lensBack focal plane of the objective lens
Aperture usedObjective aperture in the back focal plane (selects beams)Selected-area aperture in the image plane (selects region)
Screen showsMagnified image of the specimenDiffraction pattern (spots for single crystal, rings for polycrystal, diffuse halo for amorphous): SAED (selected-area electron diffraction)
InformationMorphology, defects (dislocations, grain boundaries), particle size, lattice imaging (HRTEM)Crystal structure, orientation, lattice spacings (R d = λ L, L = camera length)

Image contrast in imaging mode: Bright-field - objective aperture passes only the direct (transmitted) beam; diffracting or thick/heavy regions look dark. Dark-field - aperture passes one diffracted beam only; regions that diffract into that beam look bright. High-resolution TEM - many beams interfere (phase contrast) to image lattice fringes.

Sample preparation of a ceramic for TEM

Ceramics are hard, brittle and usually non-conducting, so they are thinned mechanically and then by ion milling until electron-transparent (< 100 nm):

Step (write this)Why / what it means
1. Cut a thin slice (~0.5-1 mm) with a low-speed diamond sawDiamond is needed for hard ceramics; slow cutting avoids cracks.
2. Core a 3 mm disc with an ultrasonic or abrasive disc cutterStandard TEM holder size.
3. Grind and polish both faces to ~100 μm with diamond lapping filmsRemoves saw damage; gives flat, parallel faces.
4. Dimple grind the centre to ~10-20 μmThins the centre while the thick rim keeps strength.
5. Argon ion milling (4-6 kV, low angle 4-8°) until a small hole forms; thin edges around it are electron-transparentIons sputter atoms gently away; ceramics cannot be electropolished as they are insulators.
6. Carbon coat the sample (thin layer)Prevents charging of the insulating ceramic in the beam.
Alternatives: FIB (focused ion beam, Ga+) lift-out of a site-specific lamella; crushing powder and dispersing on a holey-carbon grid; tripod polishingFIB is fast and site-specific; crushing is simplest for powders.

Memory trick: "Back focal plane = Diffraction, Image plane = Image"; the intermediate lens chooses. Ceramic prep: "Saw, Disc, Grind, Dimple, Ion-mill, Coat".

B1 Electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC): why high capacitance, fundamental principle Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2022 Q5(a) [12] Why does an Electric Double Layer Capacitor (EDLC) show high capacitance? Describe the fundamental principles of EDLC (electric double-layer capacitor) with necessary figure.
LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Supercapacitors, from zero

A normal capacitor stores charge on two plates separated by an insulator: C = εA/d. To store a lot you need a huge area A and a tiny gap d.

An electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC) gets both: its electrodes are activated carbon with an enormous internal surface (1000–3000 m² per gram), and the "gap" is just a layer of ions in the electrolyte sitting against the carbon surface, less than a nanometre thick. Charge is stored physically by ions lining up (no chemical reaction), so it charges in seconds and lasts a million cycles. Because d is so small and A so large, C reaches thousands of farads.

A pseudocapacitor also stores charge through fast chemical (redox) reactions at the surface of metal oxides (RuO2, MnO2) or conducting polymers: higher capacitance, but slower and shorter life.

Before you start: storing charge on a surface

A normal capacitor stores energy as charge on two metal plates separated by an insulator: C = εA/d. To store a lot, you need a huge area A and a tiny gap d.

A supercapacitor (ultracapacitor) does this with porous carbon (activated carbon has 1000-2000 m2 of surface per gram!) soaked in an electrolyte. The "gap" is only the thickness of a layer of ions, less than 1 nm. Result: thousands of times more capacitance than a normal capacitor, and much faster charging than a battery.

Electric double-layer capacitor (EDLC)

Construction: two porous high-surface-area activated carbon electrodes (also carbon nanotubes, graphene, carbide-derived carbon) coated on aluminium foil current collectors; a porous separator (paper or polymer) between them; the whole soaked in an electrolyte - aqueous (H2SO4, KOH; 1 V), organic (TEABF4 in acetonitrile; 2.7 V) or ionic liquid (3.5-4 V).

Working (charge storage mechanism):

  1. When a voltage is applied, one electrode becomes positive and the other negative.
  2. Ions of opposite charge in the electrolyte move to each electrode surface: anions to the positive electrode, cations to the negative one.
  3. At each electrode-electrolyte interface an electric double layer (Helmholtz layer) forms: the electronic charge in the carbon and a layer of ions in the electrolyte, separated by about 0.3-0.8 nm (solvent molecules).
  4. Charge is stored electrostatically - no chemical (Faradaic) reaction, no electron transfer across the interface. So charge/discharge is very fast and reversible, > 105-106 cycles.
  5. The cell is two double-layer capacitors in series: 1/Ccell = 1/C+ + 1/C−; with equal electrodes Ccell = Celectrode/2.
  6. On discharge, ions return to the bulk electrolyte and electrons flow through the external circuit.

C = εrε0A / d     E = ½CV2     Pmax = V2/(4 ESR)

Side note: Large A (porous carbon) and tiny d (one ion layer) give 100-200 F per gram of carbon. Energy rises with V2, so electrolytes with a wide voltage window (organic, ionic liquid) store more energy. ESR = equivalent series resistance.

Models of the double layer: Helmholtz (single compact layer of ions), Gouy-Chapman (diffuse layer), Stern (compact + diffuse).

Characteristics: high power density (5-10 kW/kg), modest energy density (5-10 Wh/kg, vs 100-250 for Li-ion), charging in seconds, very long life, wide temperature range, safe. Uses: regenerative braking, buses and trams, back-up memory, power smoothing for wind/solar, start-stop cars, camera flashes.

Memory trick: EDLC = "big Area (porous carbon), tiny d (ion layer), no reaction" → fast and long-life but low energy.
